power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Hearing difficulties (HD) in childhood can be associated with emotional and behavioural difficulties (EBD, including attention, peer relations, internalising symptoms, anxiety and externalising symptoms) and can have diverse impacts on educational outcomes, including mathematics.

This study has two aims: firstly, to analyse if children with HD differ from typically developing children (TD) in maths and EBD and secondly, to examine the longitudinal bidirectional relationships between maths and EBD in children with HD and TD children.

The analyses, t-test and structural equation modelling, are applied on the data of children from 5 to 11 years of age from four large longitudinal datasets from Australia (n = 2,340), the United Kingdom (n = 5,254) and two from the United States (n = 1,537 and 6,343).
The findings indicate that children with HD present with weaker maths performance, and more symptoms of EBD than TD children (Aim 1).
As for the second aim, the findings regarding the relationships between EBD at age 5 and maths at age 7/8 are inconsistent.
Attentional difficulties were consistently predictive of lower maths performance in both HD and TD children, whereas externalising symptoms were consistently unrelated to maths performance.

However, findings regarding peer relations are inconsistent for both groups of children, while higher internalising symptoms were consistently related to poorer maths only for TD children, and higher anxiety related to weaker maths performance only for HD children.
In contrast, lower performance in maths at age 7/8 was consistently related to a higher presence of EBD symptoms at age 11 for both groups.
Maths difficulties and emotional and behavioural difficulties are closely interconnected across development.

Educators and schools should therefore consider monitoring both academic performance and emotional and behavioural indicators to better identify children who may require additional classroom support or referral for further assessment.

Attentional difficulties are closely associated with maths performance across childhood, underscoring the need for educators to consider students' attentional functioning when delivering maths instruction and support.

The findings further suggest that children with hearing difficulties may be at elevated risk of experiencing both maths and emotional or behavioural difficulties, underscoring the importance of holistic educational monitoring and support across primary school.
In any given classroom, one can expect children with a broad range of abilities, including those with sensory and learning difficulties.

text.text: Maths achievement has consistently emerged as a significantly strong predictor of academic success and later employment opportunities for TD children.

There is evidence to suggest that maths abilities may be related to some measures of EBD (e.g., anxiety), but the evidence is inconsistent or lacking for other measures, such as internalising and externalising symptoms, peer problems, and victimisation.
One group of children often cited as being at higher risk of both MD and EBD is children with HD.
It is possible that the relationship between maths ability and EBD is also different (i.e., stronger or weaker association) in this population compared to children with typical hearing.
Literature on the relationship between maths ability and EBD in both children with and without HD would benefit from further research.
Therefore, the current study aimed to examine the longitudinal bidirectional relationships between maths and EBD in primary school children with and without HD.

To do so, we employed four longitudinal datasets from three countries: the Millennium Cohort Study (MCS; U.K; Hansen et al., 2014); the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC; Australia; Mohal et al., 2023); the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study: Kindergarten Class of 1998-99 (ECLS:1998; USA; Tourangeau et al., 2018); and the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study: Kindergarten Class of 2010-11 (ECLS:2011; USA; Najarian et al., 2017).

text.text: First, we examined the datasets for differences in maths ability and EBD between children with and without HD.
Based on prior literature, we expect to find a statistically significant difference in maths ability between the two groups, with lower performance in the HD group.
Given the mixed findings in the literature, we do not have specific hypotheses for the EBD variables, but we expect to find overall greater EBD in the HD group.
Next, we employed structural equation modelling to answer the following questions: 1.
What is the developmental trajectory of the relationship between maths ability and EBD in children with typical development (TD) in the earliest years of formal education?
Specifically, we examined whether EBD variables at age 5 (preschool) were related to maths ability at age 7; and if maths ability at age 7/8 was related to later EBD at age 9/11.
Is early EBD (age 5) related to maths ability (age7/8), and is maths ability related to later EBD in children with hearing difficulties (HD)?

text.text: These are described below.

The MCS consists of a stratified sample of children from the UK (n=18818) who turned 9 months-of-age between September 1, 2000, and August 31, 2001 (England and Wales) or between November 24, 2000, and January 11, 2002 (Scotland and Northern Ireland; Hansen et al., 2014).

text.text: Parent/guardian and child data were collected at 9 months, then at 1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, and 17 years.
We analysed data collected at 5, 7, and 11 years to capture pre school entry, shortly after the beginning of formal maths instruction, and later measures.
In the MCS, data related to the child was collected using computer assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) and computer assisted self-interviewing (CASI).
Questions were either open ended or consisted of a restricted set of answers.
After the field data collection, interviewers coded parent responses to medical/health questions using the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10).
The ICD-10 codes generated from parental responses relating to hearing ability in infancy, ages 1, 3, 5, and 7 were used to determine hearing status of children for this study.
We include measures from before age 5 since early HD such as repeated infections can have knock on effects even if they do not continue into the school years.
To be included in the HD group, parents must have responded "yes" to the question "Have they ever had a hearing test, were there any problems with their hearing then?"
at infancy, or the child must be identified as having ear/hearing related problems based on ICD-10 coding.

To be included in the TD group, children must have passed the hearing test at infancy (determined by parental response) and must not have any ICD-10 codes relating to ear/hearing problems (see Supplementary Material 2 in Salins et al., 2025 for ICD-10 codes used).
text.formatted: To be included in the TD group, children must have passed the hearing test at infancy (determined by parental response) and must not have any ICD-10 codes relating to ear/hearing problems (see Supplementary Material 2 in <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Salins et al., 2025</ref> for ICD-10 codes used).

text.text: Additionally, to be included in the TD group, children must not have had any reported speech difficulties, determined by the following questions: 1.
Age 3, 5 or 7: "Do you have any concerns about child's speech and language problems?"
If a parent reported any concerns other than a lisp, the child was excluded.
Age 3: "Are they understood by you (parents) at home?"
If the parent responded with 'rarely' or 'no' the child was excluded.
'Sometimes' or 'yes' was permitted.
Age 7: "Did the child receive special accommodations for speech and language problems or hearing problems?"
Excluded if the parent responded yes.
Maths.
The Progress in Maths test developed by the National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) was adapted to assess maths skills in the MCS.
The test used 20 questions to assess children's abilities in numbers, shapes, measurement, and data handling.
Children's EBD were measured using the parent report Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; Goodman, 1997).
text.formatted: Children's EBD were measured using the parent report Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Goodman, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: The SDQ provides five subscales, however we followed McArthur et al (2022) and created a set of custom subscales to align with constructs of interest here.
text.formatted: The SDQ provides five subscales, however we followed <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">McArthur et al (2022)</ref> and created a set of custom subscales to align with constructs of interest here.

text.text: McArthur et al. also reported that when attention was measured separately from other variables, the results appeared to differ, that is, the relationship with reading was driven by inattention rather than hyperactivity.
To further test this hypothesis, our subscales are identical to the ones used by Salins et al. (2025).
text.formatted: To further test this hypothesis, our subscales are identical to the ones used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Salins et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: The final subscales are peer problems (original 5 items from SDQ), anxiety (3 items from the SDQ emotional problems subscale), depression (1 item from the SDQ emotional items subscale), externalising behaviour (5 items from the SDQ conduct problems and 2 items from SDQ hyperactivity subscale) and attention (3 items from SDQ hyperactivity subscale).
After excluding samples with missing data from the variables described below, the MCS dataset consisted of 797 children with HD and 4457 with neither hearing nor speechrelated difficulties.
The LSAC consists of data from two cohorts of Australian children tested every two years from 2004 to 2014.
Testing of the Birth Cohort (B-Cohort; n = 5,107) began in their first year of life (0-1 years old); while testing of the Kindergarten Cohort (K-Cohort; n= 4,983) began at age 4 or 5.
For this study, we combined data from both cohorts at ages 4-5, 6-7, 8-9, and 10-11 (Waves 3-6 from the B-cohort and Waves 1-4 from the K-cohort).
The data from age 4-5 was used for the identification of hearing difficulty, but not in the analyses.
Children were included in the HD group if parents responded "yes" to either "Does your child have any of these ongoing conditions?
Ear infections" or "Does your child have any of these ongoing problems?
Hearing problems" in Wave C (age 4/5), Wave D (6/7), or Wave E (8/9).
To be included in the TD group, parents must have responded "no" to both those questions in all three Waves of data collection.
Additionally, parents must have responded "no" to the question, "Does your child have speech language problems at age 4/5 and 6/7; and to the question "Were they late learning to speak?"
at age 4/5.
The LSAC sample consisted of 499 children with HD and 1841 children without hearing or speechlanguage problems.
Thus, the measures of anxiety, depression, peer problems, attention, and behaviour are identical to those used in the MCS described above.
The ECLS:1998 comprises 21,260 children from the USA who were in Kindergarten in 1998 and were regularly tested from age 5 to 13 years (Grade 8; Tourangeau et al., 2009).
text.formatted: The ECLS:1998 comprises 21,260 children from the USA who were in Kindergarten in 1998 and were regularly tested from age 5 to 13 years (Grade 8; <ref type="bibr">Tourangeau et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: We used data collected during the fall term at age 5 (Kindergarten), 7 (Grade 1), and 9 (Grade 3).
Data were collected from 19,173 children at age 5, 16,593 at age 7, and 14,349 at age 9.
To classify children into HD and TD groups, we used parental responses to the question, "Does your child have difficulty hearing speech?"
at age 5 and age 7.
For the HD group, parents must have responded "yes" at (at least) one of the two time points and never responded "no".
In many instances, answers to the question above were missing for either ages 5 or 7.
To identify the TD group, parents must have said "no" at least once and never said "yes".

Additionally, they must have responded "no" to the presence of any disability at age 7 -this very conservative rule was adopted because ECLS:1998 did not provide information about the nature of any possible disabilities, and thus a response of yes, or a missing response, could indicate a hearing disability.
After excluding children with missing data for at least one variable, the sample included in the HD and TD groups were 217 and 6126 respectively.
Maths.
The focus of maths assessment was conceptual knowledge, procedural knowledge, and problem solving.
Specifically, number sense, number properties, operations, and measurement skills were assessed.
Internalising, Peer Relations, and Behaviour.
Teachers completed an adapted version of the Social Skills Rating System (Gresham & Elliot, 1990), called the Social Rating Scale (SRS).
text.formatted: Teachers completed an adapted version of the Social Skills Rating System <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Gresham & Elliot, 1990)</ref>, called the Social Rating Scale (SRS).

text.text: The modified scale included several items taken directly from the SRS, while others were modified to create four scales (self-control, interpersonal skills, externalising problem behaviours and internalising problem behaviours; Najarian et al., 2019).

text.text: For our study, we included items related to internalising problem behaviours (both anxiety and depression; n=4), externalising problem behaviours (behaviour, n=5), and peer relations (n=5; interpersonal subscale of SRS).
Teachers responded to each item on a four-point Likert scale from Never (1) to Very Often (4).

text.text: The ECLS:2011 comprises 18,174 children from the USA who were in kindergarten in 2010, and who were assessed regularly from kindergarten to Grade 5 (see Tourangeau et al., 2018, for more details).

text.text: To match the other analyses, we focused on data collected when children were aged 5 (Kindergarten fall term; n=15,756), 7 (Grade 1 spring term; n = 15,132), and 9 years (Grade 3 spring term; n=12,896).

Broadly, the analysis used the same variables as the ECLS:1998, however, a few additional measures were included, including measures of attention at all three ages, and of victimisation (bullying) and social anxiety at age 9.

Parental responses to the question "Have you obtained a diagnosis of a problem from a professional" at age 5 (Kindergarten) and age 7 (Grade 1) were used to classify children into the HD and TD groups.
A sub-sample of children underwent hearing evaluation during the fall Grade 2 data collection.

However, this data could not be used for two reasons: first, because of privacy concerns, the suppressed data is not easily accessible to researchers outside the USA; and second, because the sample size would have been too small for the modelling approach adopted here.
To be included in the HD group, parents must have responded "yes" to (at least) one of the two time points and never responded "no".
To be included in the TD group, parents must have responded "no" at both time points and "no" to the presence of any disability at age 5.

The data for the question related to speech language problems was not provided in the publicly available dataset; therefore, the broader "disability' variable was used for inclusion into the TD group.
After excluding children with missing data for any of the variables described below, the samples included in the HD and TD groups were 296 and 1241 respectively.
Bullying or Peer Victimisation.

This variable was measured with 4 items adapted from the 21-item scale of Bullying, Fighting, and Victimization (Espelage & Holt, 2001) and measured the extent to which the child was victimized (as opposed to being the bully).

text.text: The four questions related to different types of victimisation: being teased/made fun of, being the subject of false stories, being subjected to physical violence, and being left out.
Children were asked to use a 5-point rating scale ranging from 'Never' to 'Very Often' to indicate how often they experienced each type of victimisation in a school year.
The internal reliability for the 4 items was .74 in grade 3 (La Greca & Stone, 1993).
text.formatted: The internal reliability for the 4 items was .74 in grade 3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(La Greca & Stone, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Children used a 5-point scale ranging from 'Never' to 'Very Often' to rate how often they worry about what others think of them, whether others like them, and how often they are afraid others won't like them.
The reliability for the three items was .83 in third grade (age 9).

text.text: The results indicated better maths outcomes for TD across three of four datasets, with the largest difference in the ECLS:1998 dataset.
No difference was observed between the groups in NAPLAN numeracy scores in the LSAC dataset.

In terms of the EBD measures, children in the HD group consistently showed poorer attention and increased externalising symptoms compared to TD at all three time points (ages 5, 7, 9/11) in all four datasets.
They also presented with significantly higher internalising/depression symptoms compared to TD at all time points in three out of the four datasets.

text.text: The purpose of the current study was twofold; firstly, to determine whether students with HD show differences compared to hearing children in their maths ability and EBD; secondly to examine the longitudinal bidirectional relationships between maths ability and EBD in children with and without HD.
We addressed these questions using four existing datasets from three countries -USA, UK, and Australia.
Children with HD were found to perform significantly more poorly in maths than children without hearing loss in three of the four datasets.

These findings align with previous research showing lower maths achievement in children with severe-to-profound hearing loss who have not had early exposure to fluent sign language (e.g., Santos & Cordes, 2022) and those with non-permanent HD (Su et al., 2020).

text.text: Although children with HD showed overall lower scores, there was no difference found in the Australian dataset which used NAPLAN as the measure of maths ability.

Interestingly, Wang et al. (2019), also using NAPLANnumeracy scores of 11-12-year-olds (Grade 5) as the outcome measure, found that students with slight/mild unilateral or bilateral hearing loss had similar scores to hearing students.

text.text: One possibility is that, as a nationally administered assessment, appropriate adjustments are emplaced for students with recognised disabilities to support them to participate to their maximum potential; however, we cannot confirm how many students this would apply to in the current sample.
Additionally, the criteria for having a hearing difficulty from the LSAC dataset is the only one of the four datasets to include reference to ongoing ear infections.
This may have resulted in the capture of some children in the hearing difficulty group who have had ongoing ear infections but do not have associated hearing problems.
The findings for some aspects of EBD were consistent across datasets and age; children with HD were consistently rated as having poorer attention and increased externalising symptoms.
Regarding peer relations, there was a consistent pattern of poorer peer relationships for children with HD at ages 5 and 7, with the effect size in all datasets decreasing with increasing age.
By age 11, differences were seen in only two datasets (LSAC and ECLS:1998).

Stevenson et al.'s (2015) meta-analysis indicated that parents, teachers, and students themselves consistently reported higher peer problems; meta-regression for age suggested that some effects did decline with age, but not significantly so.

The exception was MCS, where they showed greater internalising problems only at age 7.

Previous studies have found differences between older and younger children, e.g., Hancock et al (2017) reported that 12-17-year-olds with hearing problems as being 3-4 times more likely to present with internalising problems; this association was not present in 4-11-year-olds once other developmental factors had been controlled for.

Australian children with HD demonstrated greater anxiety at all time points while British children with HD were reported to have greater anxiety problems only at age 7.
A third dataset, the ECLS:2011 included a measure of social anxiety at age 9, with children with HD having greater social anxiety.

Previous studies have reported that children with hearing loss are at a higher risk of developing anxiety problems than their hearing peers (Long et al., 2021; Theunissen et al., 2012 Theunissen et al., , 2014)), although this finding does not always hold when other developmental factors such as comorbid communication problems or poor health are controlled for.

text.text: Our next question addressed the directionality of relationships between maths ability and EBD, firstly whether EBD variables at age 5 are related to maths ability at age 7/8, and secondly if maths ability at age 7/8 was related to later EBD at age 9/11.

Several previous cross-sectional studies have reported on the relationship between EBD and maths but have not addressed the issue of directionality (e.g., Vieira et al., 2024), whilst others have reported a directional relationship but have not always been able to pinpoint the precise aspects of EBD that explains the relationship.

text.text: Our current analyses allowed us to more specifically isolate the aspects of EBD and address the longitudinal directionality of the relationship.
Early measures of attention (age 5) significantly and consistently predicted maths scores at age 7; better attention/fewer attention problems predicted higher maths scores.
This was observed for TD children in all three datasets that offered a measure of attention.
For HD children, this same relationship was observed in two datasets (MCS and LSAC) where attention was parent-rated, but not in ECLS:2011 where attention was teacher rated.
There were no statistically significant differences between TD and HD students in the strength of the relationship from early attention to later maths achievement.

These findings are aligned with previous research showing early assessment of attention skills and teacher and parent ratings of attention problems at ages 4-6 years significantly predict maths achievement in third grade and beyond (Duncan et al., 2007). Salla et al. (2015) also found that early childhood inattention, but not hyperactivity, significantly predicted lower teacher rated maths performance at age 12.

Unlike the other three datasets where peer / interpersonal relationships are rated by the teacher, in the MCS, peer relationships were rated by the parent.

text.text: Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged, particularly those arising from the use of secondary longitudinal datasets.
First, the classification of HD across datasets is likely to vary in accuracy and sensitivity.

In many large-scale cohort studies, hearing difficulty and loss is identified through parent report or broad screening indicators rather than clinical assessment, which may result in under-identification or misclassification.

Consequently, the current findings may be most representative of children with mild, fluctuating, or undiagnosed HD, who are often present in mainstream classrooms, but whose challenges may go unrecognised.

This is important, as these children may experience subtle but persistent difficulties in accessing linguistic input and participating in social interactions, both of which are critical for learning but are less likely to trigger formal support.

As such, the present results may underestimate the extent of difficulties faced by children with more severe or clinically identified hearing loss, while simultaneously highlighting the oftenoverlooked needs of those with less visible impairments.
Second, as with any secondary data analysis, the study is constrained by the nature and quality of the available measures, which differ across datasets.
Variability in measurement, particularly in how constructs such as EBD and academic outcomes are operationalised, may contribute to inconsistencies in findings.
However, this variability also provides a stringent test of the robustness of observed longitudinal relationships across different measurement contexts.

Notably, even after accounting for the autocorrelated nature of constructs over time, associations between EBD and maths outcomes were not always consistent, which may partly reflect differences in how maths achievement was assessed across studies (e.g., standardised tests versus curriculum-based measures).
In addition, concerns about the reliability of EBD measures, especially in early childhood, warrant consideration.
Parent-reported measures at younger ages may be less stable and more susceptible to bias, which could attenuate or obscure associations with academic outcomes.

A further limitation is the lack of control for potentially important confounding variables, such as children's reading ability and socioeconomic status (SES), both of which are known to be associated with academic outcomes and socio-emotional functioning.
The absence of these controls limits the extent to which the observed associations can be attributed specifically to HD or EBD, as opposed to broader underlying risk factors.

Furthermore, the absence of a maths outcome measure at the earliest time point limits our ability to make definitive conclusions about the unique impact of EBD on later maths ability over and above the variance accounted for earlier mathematical skills.

In addition, the present study did not examine potential gender differences which has been identified as a potential moderator in the link between emotional and behavioural difficulties and academic achievement, including maths (e.g., Dias et al., 2022; Park et al., 2025).

Together, these limitations underscore the need for future research using more precise and developmentally sensitive measures, as well as designs that can better capture the interplay between hearing status, socio-emotional functioning, and academic development.
Despite the limitations, our analysis of four large datasets has addressed several important gaps in the literature.

The findings of both maths difficulties and EBD suggest that, despite a lack of definitive information regarding formal diagnosis of hearing loss, the children classified as having HD in these four datasets do show many similarities to the performance of children with diagnosed hearing loss or those with persistent ear infections.

Importantly, these are children who may slip through the gap of educational and clinical support provisions, resulting in social and linguistic isolation and subsequent difficulties in psychopathology and learning.

Our findings also address the often-unexplored question of direction of relations between EBD and maths achievement and our focus on individual aspects of EBD allowed us to isolate specific patterns of relationships.
As found in previous research, there was a consistent pattern of maths ability at ages 7-9 years predicting all aspects of later EBD.
This was apparent for both TD children and children with HD, with a handful of findings showing stronger effects for students with HD.

A bidirectional relationship was most clearly seen in the relationship of attentional problems and mathematics; early attentional problems predicted later lower maths outcomes, which in turn predicted later attentional difficulties.
Of the other EBDs, peer relationships were also notable for similar bidirectional effects, although the findings were not as consistent as for attentional difficulties.

This raises several important implications; firstly, for children showing low maths ability in early primary school, and particularly those at greater risk of showing lower performance such as children with HD, it is important to monitor and support ongoing emotional and behavioural wellbeing alongside providing support for mathematical learning.

Furthermore, greater focus should be given to the impact of classroom inattention and poor peer relationships on later mathematical learning; again, this may be particularly important for students with HD who have greater attentional problems and poorer relationships at this young age.
It is possible that these factors interact such that attentional difficulties and less peer support result in fewer learning opportunities in the classroom.

Interventions to support early classroom attention and enhance peer relationships may be a key mechanism through which to engage young children in the important early learning opportunities that provide the foundation numerical skills for later mathematical learning.
